content: Measles is a disease caused by the Morbillivirus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. It is transmitted through respiratory secretions, such as aerosol droplets containing viral particles, which enter the respiratory tract upon contact with infected fluids. The incubation period lasts between 4 to 12 days, during which the infected individual remains asymptomatic. Symptoms typically begin with the appearance of a characteristic rash. Individuals with measles are contagious from 5 days before the rash appears until 4 days after its onset. The measles virus was first isolated in cell culture in 1954 by John F. Enders and Thomas C. Peebles. This breakthrough enabled the development of a successful vaccine, which was licensed in 1963. To date, 21 strains of the measles virus have been identified. Measles is caused by a non-segmented, negative-stranded RNA virus of the genus Morbillivirus. The primary site of infection is the respiratory epithelium of the nasopharynx. The virus is transmitted through respiratory secretions, particularly via aerosolized droplets containing viral particles. Clinically, measles is characterized by a triad of symptoms: cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis (red eyes). In most cases, the diagnosis is straightforward and can be made clinically. However, differential diagnoses should include other viral exanthems, such as erythema infectiosum and other maculopapular rashes. In regions where killed vaccines are used, atypical measles with fever, conjunctivitis, pneumonitis, and rash should be considered. Other conditions to rule out include Kawasaki disease, rubella, dengue, systemic lupus erythematosus, and serum sickness. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable childhood mortality. Global efforts, particularly through the Measles Initiative (involving organizations such as the American Red Cross, CDC, UNICEF, and WHO), have significantly reduced measles-related deaths. Between 1999 and 2005, global measles deaths decreased by 60%, with Africa experiencing a 75% reduction in annual deaths during this period. In developed countries, measles incidence is very low. However, lack of vaccination remains a significant risk factor for disease spread. In countries like the United States, most cases are linked to unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated travelers from regions with higher measles prevalence. Primary vaccine failure occurs in approximately 5% of individuals vaccinated with a single dose at 12 months of age or older, increasing their susceptibility to the disease. Measles spreads through the air via respiratory droplets from coughing, sneezing, or breathing. The virus resides in the mucus of the nose and throat of infected individuals and can survive on surfaces for up to 2 hours. It is highly contagious, and unvaccinated individuals exposed to the virus are very likely to contract the disease. Measles is a human-specific disease. Complications from measles are common and range from mild issues, such as diarrhea, to severe conditions like pneumonia and encephalitis (including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE). Adults who contract measles often experience more severe complications. While measles itself is unpleasant, its complications can be life-threatening. Between 6% and 20% of individuals with measles develop complications such as ear infections, diarrhea, or pneumonia. Approximately 1 in 1,000 individuals with measles will develop brain inflammation, and about 1 in 1,000 will die from the disease. A confirmed case of measles is diagnosed in an individual with febrile rash illness and either laboratory confirmation or a direct epidemiological link to a confirmed case. Symptoms typically begin 7 to 14 days after infection. Clinical diagnosis requires a history of fever lasting at least three days, along with at least one of the three C's—cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Koplik's spots, small white lesions on the buccal mucosa, are a characteristic finding. Fever may reach up to 104°F (40°C). Measles is best diagnosed clinically based on a constellation of signs and symptoms, including fever, rash, and conjunctivitis. Laboratory confirmation is essential for sporadic cases and outbreaks. Detection of measles-specific IgM antibodies and measles RNA via real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) are the most common methods for confirming infection. Healthcare providers should collect both serum and throat (or nasopharyngeal) swabs from suspected cases at the first point of contact. Urine samples may also contain the virus, and collecting both respiratory and urine samples can increase the likelihood of virus detection. A chest X-ray can be used to diagnose pneumonia, a common complication of measles. Findings may include patchy consolidation of lung lobes and poorly defined nodules. Other diagnostic tests include the use of Vero/hSLAM cells for virus isolation and genetic sequencing analysis. There is no specific antiviral therapy for uncomplicated measles. However, drugs such as ribavirin and interferon-α have been used in severe cases, particularly those involving central nervous system (CNS) infection. Evidence suggests that administering two doses of vitamin A to children under the age of two reduces morbidity and mortality associated with measles. For most patients, treatment focuses on supportive care. Since the introduction of the measles vaccine, there has been a dramatic reduction in disease incidence. Widespread vaccination has led to a greater than 99% reduction in measles cases in the United States compared to the pre-vaccine era. Active immunization through vaccination, often combined with rubella and mumps vaccines in the MMR vaccine, is the most effective way to prevent measles. Unfortunately, measles remains common in developing countries, where vaccination coverage is low, and the virus spreads easily across large populations. Although there is no specific antiviral treatment for measles, the significant reduction in morbidity and mortality in the United States following vaccine introduction highlights the cost-effectiveness of prevention through vaccination. Research is essential to develop better approaches to managing the disease once it is established. Additionally, creating more accessible and affordable ways to deliver vaccines to populations in developing countries could contribute to the potential eradication of measles.
